skill.name: Where the sentence ends: full stops and capitals
skill.why: A full stop tells readers to stop. Miss it and ideas crash together.
skill.how: End each whole thought with a full stop. Start the next one with a capital.

steps.say: Welcome to my kitchen diary! A sentence tells you who did something, and what they did.

show.nudge: Stirred is what happened. Who did the stirring?
The soup didn't do anything. It just got stirred!

steps.win: Yes! Mo did it, and stirred is what he did. That makes sense alone: a whole thought.

steps.say: Now my diary has two sentences, but no full stop. They crash together!

show.nudge: Mo stirred what? His sentence isn't finished yet. Read on.
The yeti and sneezed belong together. Where did Mo's sentence finish?

steps.ask: Tap where the first sentence ends.
steps.win: Yes! 'Mo stirred the soup' makes sense alone. Full stop there, then a capital: The yeti sneezed in it.

steps.say: Zed fixed it with a comma. Each part makes sense on its own. Is a comma enough?

options.text: a full stop
a comma
options.reason: That's Zed's way. A comma is only a little pause. It can't end a sentence.

options.text: nothing
options.reason: With nothing there, the two sentences crash together again.

steps.win: Right! A comma is too weak to hold two sentences apart. Use a full stop, then a capital.

steps.say: Capitals start every sentence. Names, days and the word I get one too, even in the middle.

show.nudge: Is lodge a name, or just a kind of building? Look for a name or a day.
Soup is just food. Is it a name, a day or I?

steps.ask: Tap the word that needs a capital letter.
steps.win: Yes! Friday is the name of a day, so it gets a capital F. Gus and I have theirs.

steps.say: Careful! Gus wants a full stop in the middle of this one. Say the first part alone.
show: When the battery died, the robot froze.

options.text: one
two
options.reason: Say 'When the battery died' alone. Does it make sense, or leave you waiting?

options.text: none
options.reason: 'The robot froze' makes sense on its own. So there is at least one.

steps.win: Yes! 'When the battery died' leaves you waiting. It hangs on to the rest. One sentence, one full stop.

steps.say: Your turn. Gus wrote this about my cake. Find where the crash is.

show.nudge: Gus dropped what? His sentence isn't finished yet. Read on.
Landed is what 'it' did. That sentence is still going. Look earlier.

steps.ask: Tap where the full stop goes.
steps.win: Yes! 'Gus dropped the cake' makes sense alone. Full stop there, and It gets a capital.

terms.means: Says who did what and makes sense on its own. Ends with a full stop.
Starts every sentence. Names, days and the word I get one too.

card.test: Who did what, and makes sense alone? Full stop, never a comma. Then a capital.

creature.name: Dotumble
creature.blurb: A mountain pygmy possum that curls into a perfect full stop to sleep through winter. It only wakes when a capital letter knocks.

write.ask: Fix these words into two sentences. Then write one more sentence of your own about the dog.
given: gus dropped the cake on friday it landed on the dog

Each sentence ends with a full stop, not a comma
